#4770. Taking Blood Pressure Meds? DASH Diet Likely Safe for Potassium Levels

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who adhere to the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet do not experience significant changes in potassium levels while taking blood pressure medications or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drugs, according to a new study.

Researchers also reported that people taking these medications do not experience significant changes in their kidney function.

Both types of medications are known to increase potassium levels. High potassium levels can lead to hyperkalemia, a condition that can cause issues with the heart rhythm. People with impaired kidney function due to chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of hyperkalemia.

“The DASH diet is a well-known, proven nutrition pattern that is known to improve blood pressure,” said Marian Budu, MD, a clinical research coordinator on the GoFresh Trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and the presenting author of the study, in a news release.

“Knowing that the DASH diet did not increase blood potassium levels in this population with normal baseline potassium levels provides assurance that the DASH diet can be prescribed to a wide range of people,” she continued.

The preliminary findings are being presented at the American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026 meeting this week in Virginia. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the research provides medical professionals with important information.

“While we have traditionally exercised caution before recommending the DASH diet in patients who are prescribed ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or potassium-sparing diuretics, these results show that those patients could likely adopt the DASH diet without significant concern for harm,” said Cheng-Han Chen, MD, an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA.

“DASH diets do not appear to increase potassium levels to any significant degree in patients taking medications that are known to potentially raise serum potassium,” added Kevin Volpp, MD, the founding director of the Penn Center for Health Incentives and Behavioral Economics in Pennsylvania and the scientific lead of the American Heart Association’s Health Care by Food initiative.

“This is important because it is a theoretical concern that diets rich in potassium could cause high levels in potassium in some patients.”

The new study was a secondary analysis of the GoFresh and GoFresh Rx randomized trials that enrolled Black adults in the greater Boston area with high blood pressure.

Some of the participants were taking medications to lower their blood pressure, and others were not taking any hypertension drugs.

The study focused on four classes of blood pressure medications: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and potassium-sparing diuretics and beta-blockers, as well as NSAIDs.

The analysis took place in 2026 and included 356 Black adults with an average age of 53. About 70% were women.

At the start of the study, the participants had systolic blood pressure readings between 120 mm Hg and less than 150 mm Hg. They also had a diastolic blood pressure reading of less than 100 mm Hg.

The participants also had varying degrees of kidney function. In addition, they had limited access to grocery stores.

Half of the participants received three months of weekly DASH-patterned groceries and weekly nutrition counseling sessions. The other half received a cash stipend every four weeks to buy groceries, with no nutrition counseling.

The participants’ blood potassium levels were measured at the beginning of the study and again after 12 weeks.

The researchers reported that eating more potassium-rich foods in the DASH diet did not increase potassium levels to dangerous levels among participants taking blood pressure medications.

They noted no significant increase in potassium levels, regardless of whether participants were assigned to the dietary intervention or the monetary stipend group.

In a news release, the researchers acknowledged that their study did not include people with stage 4 or stage 5 kidney disease or those with higher-than-normal potassium levels.

They added that the study population comprised only Black individuals living in Boston, so the results may not generalize to the broader population.

The study authors said that future research should focus on participants with suboptimal kidney function and those with higher potassium levels.

Volpp agreed that more research is needed.

“This study was conducted in patients with non-elevated potassium levels at baseline and does not answer the question of whether they are safe in patients with elevated potassium levels or significant impairments in renal function,” he told Healthline.

Chen noted that potassium levels should be taken seriously.

“Certain classes of blood pressure medications can potentially cause high potassium levels, especially in people with kidney disease,” he told Healthline. “If potassium levels become too high, this can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and muscle pain, or even serious heart problems such as arrhythmias.”

The DASH diet is a dietary plan that emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins such as chicken, fish, and beans.

The plan also includes whole grains, low fat dairy products, and cooking with vegetable oils. The diet discourages the intake of red meat, salt, fat, and added sugars.

Previous research has indicated that the DASH diet can provide numerous health benefits.

A preliminary 2022 study concluded that the dietary plan can help lower blood pressure and improve heart health, but those results haven’t been published in a scientific journal. Still, the findings were consistent with a 2019 study that found the DASH diet can help lower the risk of heart disease.

In addition, a 2020 study reported that adults aged 65 and older with obesity lost body fat while following the DASH Diet. A 2023 study suggested the diet can help reduce belly fat.

A 2019 meta-analysis suggested that the DASH diet may also help lower the risk of certain cancers.

Many of these protective effects are attributed to the diet’s high fruit and vegetable content.

Chen said the DASH diet has many benefits, but the eating plan might not be for everybody.

“The DASH diet has been shown to be beneficial in lowering blood pressure, losing weight, and controlling blood sugar and cholesterol levels,” he said. “However, the amount of planning and portion tracking required to follow the diet may be too much for some people.”

Chen recommended that people ease into the DASH diet.

“The best way to start on the DASH diet is to slowly introduce the changes to your meals,” he said. “This can be as simple as including a few extra servings of fruits and vegetables each day as well as swapping some whole grain products for refined grains. Over time, more of the diet can be incorporated.”

Volpp agreed that introducing the DASH diet in increments is a good strategy.

“For many people, it is easiest to make small incremental changes sequentially,” he said. “One way to get started is to increase fruit by a couple of servings a day. Another is to pay attention to the amount of sodium in packaged foods and consciously choose products lower in sodium. A third is to make a conscious effort to eat more vegetables.”

“Make changes first that are easiest for you to make; it will be easier to make those changes stick,” Volpp added.

#4769. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4768. How Shame Can Drive Crime

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Shame is often said to be the most powerful emotion. We have all felt the sharp pain of shame: the fear that we are not good enough. “Shame strikes deepest into the heart of man…it is an inner torment, a sickness of the soul…” (Sedgwick & Frank, as cited in George, 2025).

Shaming can—and does—occur every day in parent-child relationships as a means of communicating that a behavior is undesirable or unacceptable, helping children learn social norms. Its inhibitory effect can be protective. Although such moments may be difficult, this kind of corrective shaming is most often followed by a restoration of connection with the parent and reassurance that bad behavior does not define the child as bad or unacceptable.

Early shame expressions have been observed in infants as young as 7 months, and self-awareness emerges in the second year of life (George, 2025), during the phase identified by Erik Erikson as “Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt.” The central tasks during toddlerhood are learning to do things on one’s own and developing skills, self-control, and self-confidence. When caregivers are overly restrictive, harsh, or critical, the shame that arises can instead lead to self-doubt and low self-esteem.

Serious problems arise when withdrawal of love accompanies shaming, and the “bad” behavior is not differentiated from the person of the child, leading to a more global sense of being flawed or unlovable as a human being. Unbearable feelings of shame can follow. A young child whose parent turns away or conveys contempt or indifference must find a way to manage without the parent’s help. There is no repair to provide relief, reconnection, and the ability to move forward.

Shame is biologically stressful. The flood of painful emotion inhibits speech and thought, and the person feels acutely self-conscious, small, and exposed (Herman, 2018). Children erect defenses to protect themselves from the pain of devaluation of the self. They may become enraged, turning the discomfort of self-blame into blaming others. They may become perfectionistic, hoping that being perfect will protect them from criticism and rejection. They may withdraw from other people, finding safety in isolation.

Child abuse, such as violence or the threat of violence, control of bodily functions, or degradation, subjects children to shame states that are overwhelming. They experience “an intense and destructive sense of self-disgust, verging on self-hatred” when they are treated as a physical object by those who would be expected to love and care for them (Fonagy et al., 2003, as cited in Herman, 2018). These powerful feelings of self-hate do not evaporate and are easily set off by future events.

We know that childhood maltreatment is associated with risk for committing future violence among juveniles and adults. Hypothesized links between violence and childhood abuse include learning violent behavior from parents, effects of trauma on brain development and functioning, including dysregulation of the stress response system and deficits in self-regulation (Miley, Fox, Muniz et al., 2020; Burke, Ellis, Peltier, et al., 2023). There is little in the literature that examines the contribution of the shame that arises from experiences of child abuse, but I believe it is an invisible contributor more often than we think.

Significant levels of shame can lead to withdrawal or to greater externalizing and aggressive tendencies (Maggi, Zaccaria & Breda et al., 2022). People who suffer pervasive feelings of devaluation and inadequacy fear exposure of the devalued self and mask it with acts of aggression. I saw this in juvenile offenders I interviewed for my book, Before Their Crimes: What We’re Misunderstanding about Childhood Trauma, Youth Crime, and the Path to Healing.

One boy, Simon (not his real name), routinely brutally beaten by his father, was infuriated when some younger members of his gang refused to do his bidding during a confrontation with another gang. “I felt I needed to prove myself, not only to myself, but to the younger guys. I said f*ck it, and I pulled the trigger.” In a moment, his life and that of another boy ended tragically.

Carl (another pseudonym) was physically abused by his mother throughout childhood. The family had modest means, and as a teenager, Carl was intensely ashamed as he compared himself to other kids. He felt compelled to begin stealing to acquire clothes and objects that assuaged a profound sense of inferiority and inadequacy.

A second way that shame is sometimes a factor in aggression and violence is that it impairs the development of the capacity for empathy (Maggi, Zaccaria & Breda et al., 2022). Empathy develops in and through relationships in which we feel seen, heard, and loved. Maltreated children have instead been harshly treated in a context where empathic response is absent.

Most children are unable to manage traumatic experiences or overwhelming shame on their own. Unmanageable feelings must be kept at bay and people at a distance to protect the vulnerable self. If you can’t allow people close to you, there is no chance to develop relationships that might be reparative. When you cannot permit your own feelings, the feelings of others are not real to you. You don’t see your victims as human beings like yourself, but as threats or enemies that must be defeated or destroyed.

When abused children turn to crime, the traumatic nature of maltreatment plays a central role in disrupting normal development. We should not forget that the shame of feeling unlovable and devalued that accompanies abuse compounds the damage and finds its way into the dire strategies meant to protect the shattered sense of self.

Burke, C., Ellis, J. D., Peltier, M. R., Roberts, W., Verplaetse, T. L., Phillips, S., ... & McKee, S. A. (2023). Adverse childhood experiences and pathways to violent behavior for women and men. Journal of interpersonal violence, 38(3-4), 4034-4060.

George, C. (2025). Attachment, shame, and trauma. Brain Sciences, 15(4), 415.

Herman, J. L. (2018). Shattered shame states and their repair. In Shattered states (pp. 157-170). Routledge.

Maggi, S., Zaccaria, V., Breda, M., Romani, M., Aceti, F., Giacchetti, N., ... & Sogos, C. (2022). A narrative review about prosocial and antisocial behavior in childhood: The relationship with shame and moral development. Children, 9(10), 1556.

Miley, L. N., Fox, B., Muniz, C. N., Perkins, R., & DeLisi, M. (2020). Does childhood victimization predict specific adolescent offending? An analysis of generality versus specificity in the victim-offender overlap. Child Abuse & Neglect, 101, 104328.

And while I try a lot of compression leggings and moisture-wicking underwear that blow me away, I also try some not-so-great stuff that makes their way to the bottom of my dresser or giveaway pile.

But what truly sets lululemon apart is its obsessive attention to detail—from sweat-wicking fabrics that feel like a second skin to precision tailoring that moves with you. Our fashion editors agree: these pieces don’t just last, they become essentials you can’t live without.

One downside of lululemon's activewear is that it errs on the pricier side, but our editors definitely think they’re worth the investment, since lululemon excels at durability. In terms of the pieces we love, the Lululemon Align Leggings can’t go without a shout-out. Our editors love them for their breathability, barely-there feel, and how easy they are to move in thanks to the perfect blend of stretchy elastane and smooth nylon. All of those features extend to its other activewear, like sweat-wicking tops, biker shorts, sports bras, and more.

Another loved product by Vitola and our team? The cult-classic Energy Bra, which is one of our all-time favorite sports bras, is especially great for medium-impact activity like strength training or jogging. "It’s super comfortable on my shoulders and doesn’t give me a uni-boob under my shirts," she says, adding that she likes that the cross straps take the pressure off your shoulders during wear.

Crz Yoga Butterluxe Cross Waist Workout Leggings

Since Crz Yoga’s prices are more budget-friendly, I was a little skeptical about the quality. But after trying the Butterluxe Workout Leggings, I was surprised—they’re almost as comfortable as our top pick, lululemon. And at half the price, they’re an even easier buy.

Vuori is another personal favorite on this list, as its fabric is unbelievably soft without slacking on compression. Vuori not only hugs you in all the right places, but the textures are so soft against your skin (hi, polyester and elastane blend), says personal trainer Kim Strother, NASM, who also loves the brand's Daily Collection. Gini Grimsley, MS, director of fitness products at Vasa Fitness, is a big fan of Vuori's famed Performance Joggers because they allow for a ton of movement without needing to readjust the waistband. As a weightlifter, she never has to adjust her clothing between sets, meaning she has more time to focus on the task at hand. Vuori’s proprietary fabric is so comfy that we’ve even worn its leggings for couch rotting, lounging, errands, and the list goes on.

I did notice that Vuori's sizing is not as inclusive as other brands on this list, with most of its options only ranging from XXS to 2X (as a reference, Girlfriend Collective's options go all the way to a 6X!).

I’ve been testing activewear for years, but it was not until recently that I gave Athleta a shot, and it has quickly become one of my all-time favorite activewear brands. Golf instructor Erica Larkin loves Athleta's layering pieces and outerwear—like its pullovers and jackets—as they keep her dry and warm during every season. Plus, they're easy to move and swing in. Taryn Toomey, founder and creative director of The Class, agrees. She loves moving in a way that lets her focus on how her body feels, not her clothes—and Athleta’s gear makes that easy.

Popflex is another brand that I’ve always known about, but never put to the test until recently. Who knew they had the cutest designs? (Everyone but me? Oops!). The brand was founded by Cassey Ho in 2016 after taking YouTube by storm with her super popular “Blogilates” Pilates videos. Cassey’s designs are not only super stylish, but they also feel and function like clothes I want to work out in—which isn’t always the case with cute activewear. Both the bra and shorts stay in place through whatever crazy movements my Pilates instructor has on the agenda, and the material is so comfortable. I love that the shorts don’t have a front seam (most of Popflex’s bottoms don’t!) to avoid an unflattering cameltoe. Plus, the crisscross design on the front of the shorts and the back of the bra is also just extremely stylish and makes getting dressed for a workout class fun.

Popflex activewear also comes in at a super reasonable price point. I’ve gotten my sweat on in similar pieces (both in terms of style and material) that cost more than double, and my Popflex pieces make a very good argument for spending less. They perform well during intense workouts and in sweaty, heated classes while holding up against pilling and shrinkage after numerous washes.

Nike Pro Sculpt High-Waisted 7/8 Leggings

When it comes to activewear, there's a high chance you have at least one Nike piece in your closet—at least WH editors all do. The brand is a go-to for classic styles and reliable basics, with its pieces ranging from practical gym ‘fits to streetwear staples. We especially like that Nike's sizing is pretty solid, with pieces ranging from size XS to 3XL. I'm a true medium (typically a size six in clothing), and all of Nike's medium sizes fit me like a glove, so I can also attest to the brand's size consistency.

In our opinion, it blends streetwear (hi, bold branding, oversized fits, and trend-driven designs) with performance to make functional pieces that are designed for movement. "No matter what I have on-deck, its styles easily morph into any occasion from being in the studio or out and about." We’ve even worn some of its clothing to spruce up a GNO.

Coleman specifically loves the Zenvy Legging (I'm also a huge fan of these—they’re lightweight and squat-proof!), the Alate Sports Bra, and her all-time favorite training shoe, the Nike Free Metcon 6. What specifically draws Coleman to Nike is its representation and diversity as a brand and in its products. "It also pushes the envelope on innovation and partners with some of the most talented athletes in the world," she says.

Registered dietitian Maddie Pasquariello, RDN, has had a longtime obsession with Splits59 because its products hold up better than any others she owns. She says she's owned one of the brand's leggings for five years (!!), and they've retained their shape, stretch, and color the entire time.

Pasquariello also adds that she prefers matte fabrics over shiny ones, and Splits 59 has many options that are up her alley. Plus, we especially love the colors and patterns the clothes are available in, all options that are easy to mix and match.

While Pasquariello loves everything she's tried from the brand, she calls out the Ella High Waist Airweight Legging as well as the matching Ella Airweight Bra—they’re made out of moisture-wicking and quick-drying nylon that keep you comfortable during super sweaty workouts. And don't sleep on the stretchy tanks and tees—the Jackson Rib Turtleneck is so cute and it has thumb holes, which makes it perfect for chillier days, she notes.

Girlfriend Collective Compressive Pocket Run Short

Wang loves Girlfriend clothing specifically for yoga, touting the Float line as the fabric is slightly thicker and more compressive for flexible moves like downward dog or child’s pose. While its clothes are slightly more expensive, she says she sees Girlfriend Collective as an investment in quality, comfort, and inclusive sizing. Style coach Liz Wendler is also a fan of the brand, calling out its Compressive Leggings and Paloma Racerback Bra. "This set is incredibly comfortable and sits at the right spot for comfort and movement," she says.

I do find that its sizing runs a tad bit big, so if you want your workout attire to fit more on the snug side, opt for a size down than what you’d normally go for.

The brand’s signature FormFlex fabric (a blend of smooth nylon and stretchy elastane), which you can find in most of the line, is buttery-soft and breathable with light support. Alo is always ahead of the curve when it comes to fashion-forward activewear. And, that’s why it’s the most widely worn brand among our editors. We appreciate the brand because the quality of its clothing is consistently top-notch, its sizing is inclusive, and its pieces hold up through all kinds of activities.

Saladino loves that the brand makes a little bit of everything—biker shorts perfect for hot yoga or summer workouts, recovery sneakers, smoothing leggings, and the list goes on. And, we love that it introduces new, fun colors every month so its products never get old and there’s always an option for anyone.

The brand offers three signature fabrics: Airlift (82% polyester, 18% elastane), Airbrush (87% nylon, 13% elastane), and Alosoft (87% polyester, 13% elastane). Each one has a different feel—whether you want high compression, extra softness, or more stretch. This makes shopping at Alo a breeze, and once you find a fabric you love, you can stick with it and grab different styles in the same material.

Like many of the other brands on this list, Adanola offers a variety of styles that work with different dress codes from the gym to the office. But, we also love that most of its pieces are below $100. And DW, the quality is surprisingly great for the price.

Adanola is a favorite in fitness instructor Aubre Winters-Casiano's closet. Its apparel is simple yet makes you feel like the coolest and most confident gal in the room, she says. I’ve worn its clothes to the gym, but I also own pieces perfect for lounging around my apartment.

Winter-Casiano's favorite pieces are the Ultimate Tank Bra, the Ultimate Leggings, and the Ultimate Long Sleeve Longline Top. "The Ultimate Sleeveless Unitard is also so flattering," she adds. She also calls out that the brand shows its pieces on models of all different body types and shapes, which makes her feel really confident ordering online while pregnant.

Saladino says that its fabric feels thick and super high-quality. For the leggings specifically, the high-waisted band stays securely in place without any need for adjustments during yoga. “I most often reach for its flared leggings—they’re my go-to for barre class, especially when I’m wearing ankle weights.” And, on weekends, she reaches for them just to lounge because they’re just that comfortable. She even ended up buying two more pairs so she always has a clean option in her drawer.

Both Lauture and I are obsessed with the adorable styles from FP Movement. We can confidently say we’ve never felt more stylish—whether we’re working out, hiking, running, or just lounging. The pieces pair effortlessly with anything, but the subtle boho flair and vibrant, versatile colors make them stand out. Plus, its quality is amazing—its workout sets are extremely soft and maintain their quality after multiple washes, Lauture says.

I also love the versatility of FP Movement. In my mind, it’s less of a workout brand and more of a lifestyle label because there are so many clothing options to choose from. I own the extremely soft and stretchy Never Better Full-Length Leggings, but I also have outerwear like the Mountain Top Half Zip Fleece and cozies like the For The Win Sleeveless Sweatshirt and the Let’s Bounce Pant.

If you want ultra-high-performance gear, FP Movement might not be your best bet. But if you're after everyday staples that can take you from the gym to the rest of your day while keeping you effortlessly cute, it's a solid choice.

The professionals on this list agree: The best workout clothes should be comfortable. But because sweat does happen while you're working out, they recommend materials that are moisture-wicking, like nylon or elastane.

I'm gonna be honest—some of the brands on this list can get a little pricey (hi, lululemon and Vuori). But, the pros recommend them because they're long-lasting, and they feel stretchy and soft rather than heavy and constricting. If you're looking for something on the more affordable side, check out Amazon’s exclusive workout brands or Adanola, which has many stylish options for less than $100.

Speaking of long-lasting wear, you want to make sure your workout clothes won't pill, stretch, or lose their color after a few wears and washes. All the brands on this list have passed that test. Registered dietitian Maddie Pasquariello, RDN, has even owned the same pair of leggings from Splits59 for five years and says they're still good as new.

Besides their ability to stay intact for years, you also want to make sure your workout clothes pass the wear test. Do they allow for movement? Are they see-through while squatting or bending over? Does the waistband slide down? You can get a good sense of whether or not your activewear passes the wear test by trying it on in person before you make a purchase.

#4766. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Lung Cancer Can Look Like Anyone

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Picture someone with lung cancer. Now picture a 24-year-old soccer player in the prime of his life. A filmmaker in her early 40s with a camera in her hand, doing what she loves best. A busy mom of two, with a shoulder so sore she can’t pick up her newborn, yet struggling to get a diagnosis.

The gap between the picture in our heads and the people actually being diagnosed is costing time. And time is the one thing with lung cancer you cannot get back.

We know that lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the leading cause of cancer death. And while lung cancer incidence rates are falling in many countries as fewer people smoke, lung cancer in people who have never smoked is on the rise globally, both as a proportion and in absolute numbers.

According to the CDC, as many as 20% of lung cancers diagnosed in the US are in people who have never smoked. Data suggests that non-smoking lung cancer is now among the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide.

The numbers are stark. Lung cancer can affect anyone. And that includes the young – like Alex, one of the subjects of a powerful new short documentary commissioned by the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK for their Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign.

Alex was a 24-year-old soccer player who died just weeks after receiving a diagnosis of Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) positive lung cancer, following several misdiagnoses born of the fact that no one suspected lung cancer in one so young, fit, and with no smoking history. The film was made by filmmaker Sarah Li, who herself was diagnosed with Stage 4 EGFR+ lung cancer in April 2024, just a month after Alex died from the same mutation of the disease, and charts her journey with survivor’s guilt, what an earlier diagnosis may have meant for Alex, and what that fact means for her own future.

Ahead of Lung Cancer Awareness Month in November, I sat down with my friend, Gini Harrison, to talk about the film, her own journey, and why catching lung cancer sooner matters so much. Gini is a Professor of Psychology at The Open University, a trustee of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK, and is living with stage 4 EGFR-positive lung cancer. She’s also the mom at the top of this piece, whose sore shoulder was initially attributed to breastfeeding posture.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Gini Harrison: I’d had my son, Michael, in February 2021 and was on maternity leave. My daughter, Emily, was five. I think the shoulder pain started around March, but that was it. No cough, no breathlessness… nothing that made me think about my lungs.

Initially, they gave me painkillers, which helped a bit. But the pain kept getting worse. Eventually, I started losing movement and strength in my arm, and it got to the point where I couldn’t pick up my son anymore.

This was all happening during COVID, so my appointments were over the telephone. Eventually, after months without being examined face-to-face, I paid to see a shoulder specialist. As soon as he touched my shoulder blade and I practically leaped out of the chair, he knew something wasn’t right. He ordered an MRI, which showed a tumor in my shoulder blade and another in my upper right lung. In December 2021, I was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer.

Gini Harrison: I wasn’t thinking, “This must be cancer.” I was just thinking, “Why isn’t this getting better?”

And I think that distinction matters. Patients shouldn’t have to identify their own disease before they can get help. You should be able to say that something is wrong and be listened to.

Gini Harrison: It was devastating. So many of my first questions were about the children: “How are we going to tell them?” “Am I going to be here to see them grow up?” “Will they remember me?” Suddenly, there was a question mark over a future I’d taken for granted.

I was also completely shocked by the type of cancer. If someone had said breast cancer, I don’t think I would have been anywhere near as surprised. But lung cancer?! I’d always associated it with smoking, and I’d never smoked.

I hadn’t imagined that this particular cancer could ever happen to me. So yes, I had some assumptions that I now challenge. I understand how deeply rooted they are because I had them too.

Gini Harrison: People are often shocked, and one of the first questions is whether I smoked.

And they often look healthy. That doesn’t mean everything is easy, or that there aren’t side effects. It just means you can’t tell what someone is dealing with by looking at them.

I think we’ve given lung cancer such a narrow public image that people outside it can become almost invisible.

Gini Harrison: Oh, yes! Once, I spoke to a doctor about a breathing problem after radiotherapy. He asked, “How much did you smoke?” When I said I’d never smoked, he replied, “Well, how did you get lung cancer then?”

On another occasion, I went to a hospice for help managing side effects, and someone there asked, “How are you still alive?” That’s quite a thing to hear when you’ve come looking for support!

When people ask about smoking, I try to explain that I’ve never smoked and I’m certainly not alone. Never smoking doesn’t make you immune. But I’m also very clear that nobody deserves lung cancer, whether they’ve smoked or not. We shouldn’t be creating a hierarchy of who deserves compassion.

Smoking history matters medically. But in a personal conversation, “How are you doing?” is a much kinder place to start.

Gini Harrison: Lung cancer isn’t one single disease. Two people can both have lung cancer, but different changes in their cells may be driving it.

Genes contain the instructions that tell our cells how to work, including when to grow and divide. Changes in those genes (called mutations) can cause cells to keep dividing when they shouldn’t, forming a tumor. In my case, there’s a mutation in a gene called EGFR.

EGFR-positive lung cancer is a type of non-small cell lung cancer caused by a genetic mutation in the EGFR gene, which keeps the EGFR receptor switched “on,” leading to uncontrolled cell growth and enhanced cancer cell survival.

Biomarker testing looks for these changes, as well as other features of the cancer that can guide treatment. If we know what’s helping the cancer grow, there may be a medication that specifically targets it.

The word “genetic” can sound scary, particularly when you have children. But these changes usually develop in cancer cells over a person’s lifetime. They aren’t necessarily inherited.

Gini Harrison: Please get it checked. And if it persists, worsens or doesn’t improve with treatment, go back. Explain what’s changed and how it’s affecting your life. Ask, “What happens next if this doesn’t get better?”

The symptoms don’t always look like lung symptoms. Mine was shoulder pain.

Most symptoms will turn out to be something other than cancer. But when a symptom continues to worsen, the original explanation needs to be reconsidered. Lower risk doesn’t mean no risk.

And I don’t want all the responsibility to fall on patients to keep pushing. Reassurance should come with a next step.

Gini Harrison: Once I had recovered from my initial treatment, I realized that I wanted to help others in my situation, so I became a trustee of the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK. Through this work, we produced a film, Our Lungs: Time to Breathe. At the heart of it, it challenges the perception of what someone with lung cancer looks like.

The hardest part is how close to home it feels. Alex was so young, and that worked against him. Watching his family talk about what happened is heartbreaking. It’s just so unfair.

Gini Harrison: Sarah’s story shows life continuing alongside lung cancer. She’s a filmmaker with ambitions, people she loves, and things she wants to do.

Through Alex’s family, you see the enormity of the loss. I hope people feel that, rather than simply hearing another statistic.

Gini Harrison: For me, the biggest thing is that my children are growing up and I’m here to see it. Michael is now five (the age Emily was when I was diagnosed), and Emily is about to turn ten. I can’t tell you how grateful I am to be here with them.

It wasn’t about big bucket-list things. It was about being here every day. Seeing Michael start school. Seeing Emily reach double figures. Those milestones are enormous when you’ve wondered whether you’d get to see them.

After chemotherapy and radiotherapy, I’ve had no evidence of disease since May 2022, and my scans remain stable. But a big change has been seeing the progress in available treatment. It gives me more hope about what might be available if I need treatment again.

The public image of lung cancer still needs to catch up. We need better recognition of symptoms, access to appropriate testing and treatment, and support for the whole person. As a psychologist as well as a patient, I’m particularly aware that psychological well-being and family life need attention alongside the cancer itself.

Gini Harrison: I’d love for people to share the film and help get it in front of those who wouldn’t normally think lung cancer has anything to do with them. And take something from it into everyday life: book the appointment you’ve been putting off, ask your doctor about testing, or respond with kindness when someone tells you about their diagnosis.

Just being willing to rethink your assumptions could make a difference.

Gini Harrison: “You don’t have to put a brave face on with me. How are you really doing?”

When you look well, or your scans are good, people can assume you’re “fine now”. But I’m not sure the fear ever completely goes away. Every scan is terrifying. It feels like there’s a sword of Damocles hanging over my head, and part of me is waiting for the bad scan. I also still have lasting side effects from treatment, and probably always will.

My life has fundamentally changed. Some of that has brought good things, but it doesn’t make the difficult parts disappear. It helps when someone gives you room to be honest about both, without expecting you to reassure them or turn everything into a positive story.

Gini and I have been friends for nearly 30 years, and, while she’d probably cringe to hear me say it, I remain in awe of the way she approaches life with cancer. I am so grateful for her sharing her experiences with me for this column. What Gini asks of us is simple: look again, ask the question, listen, and act on your instincts. Our Lungs: Time to Breathe is where that starts for her. You can learn more about the Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign and the wider work of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK by clicking the links. — Robin Hough

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4764. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4763. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4762. Downsizing Isn’t for Everyone

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As we grow older, we face considerable pressure to reduce our possessions and our living space. Such downsizing can have practical benefits and be personally liberating, but it can also lead to unnecessary stress and guilt.

This post does not criticize the act of downsizing, but it does push back against the pressure to do so, especially for the sake of our children. We can declutter and live more simply, but we should not feel obligated or guilted into discarding what is valuable to us.1

Downsizing is often promoted as a virtuous gift and a way of showing love to our heirs. As middle-aged and elderly adults, we are counseled to reduce clutter so our children won’t face the arduous task of clearing out and cleaning after we die. We are also advised not to accumulate any new things because of the additional burden this will add.2

In an enlightening post on Swedish Death Cleaning, Psychology Today blogger Dr. Donelle Dreese offers a different perspective, saying that such cleaning “is an act of love for all those who will be in the position to clean out our ‘stuff’ after we are gone.”

Disciplined downsizing is also presented as a path to wisdom. By going through all of our possessions, seriously considering what matters to us and discarding the rest, we may move toward a deeper understanding of our place on Earth, “growing downward, smaller, one among the grasses,” in the words of poet Wendell Berry. Such downsizing conveys a moral imperative to acquire wisdom through un-acquiring possessions.

Considering the Children. For many of us, when we die, our children will be in middle age. The ideas in Swedish death cleaning and in KonMari about being a good ancestor are thoughtful and inspiring, but we are not in the best position to examine each of our possessions and determine its future personal value for others or its potential to give joy. Our middle-aged children will be quite capable of assessing what is or is not valuable to them.

In fact, grown children may discover interesting artifacts that tell them more about their parents. My father, for example, kept a file of published cartoons that my sister and I had never seen, left over from his young adulthood as an amateur cartoonist.

Considering Ourselves. If the things we own give us joy and pleasure, why not keep them? Our possessions are not disposable content.

I have small, unnecessary collections of first editions of poetry and memoir, which I enjoy seeing as I walk past them on the bookshelf, occasionally taking down one of the books and slowly reading.

And if something new comes along that delights us, then why not consider getting it?

Nurturing Future Generations. For many older adults, extra living space bestows hope that our grandchildren and grown children will visit and need guest rooms. Two of my grandchildren are now old enough to visit on their own—which they have done—and my extra bedrooms set up a more inviting environment.

In general, as we grow older, we want autonomy with our belongings and living spaces. According to the AARP, nearly 90 percent of adults over 65 want to age in place whenever possible, in their current homes and with their own belongings.

Preserving Our Past. A pioneering study by Margaret Boschetti documented that cherished possessions contribute to our self concepts about who we are and what we’ve done. They help us remember important experiences, relationships, and identities of the past.

Looking Around and Looking Ahead. In a 2020 study, Tara Coleman and Janine Wiles found connections with belongings that transcend the past. The majority of participants in this study interacted with cherished possessions not only to connect with their past selves but also to cope with times of challenge and change in the present and to cultivate a sense of aging in place in the future.

Individual Differences. Research conducted by Mary Dozier and Catherine Ayers in 2021 showed that object attachment exists across our life span, with fluctuations in levels of attachment. For healthy management of possessions, there isn’t one fixed strategy across individuals or even within an individual.

Easily accessed possessions can provide comfort, affirming our preferred self concepts and improving our quality of life. Or they can disrupt our sense of self. The unplayed upright piano in our living room may reinforce our self concept of being musical. Or it may regularly remind us of what we’ve lost. There are no general rules about such possessions. We need to assess their personal value in our own way.

Most of us want to downsize as we get older, even if we find it difficult. How should we approach the management of our possessions?

1) Focus on what to keep, instead of what to throw away. Ask what items matter most or what stories lie behind cherished objects.

2) Begin by clearing out the more obvious, low-emotion areas first, such as the basement, attic, or garage. When considering the living room or bedrooms, we should give ourselves time and many iterations.

3) Before substantially downsizing, seek information and support from peers who have gone through the same thing.

4) Avoid an “Antiques Roadshow” perspective. The potential value of our possessions is not a sound reason for keeping them—unless they are appraised works of art or age-worthy bottles of wine. Chances are, they are not objectively valuable or not easily sold as individual items.

5) Research the cost of companies in the area that manage the clearing out, donating, and selling of belongings. Include that amount in a will for that particular purpose.3

Downsizing decisions may be easier than anticipated. My sump pump has broken twice in the past eight years during heavy rain, resulting in two basement floods and two separate clear outs. The first clear out was easy because only my low priority possessions were sitting on the basement floor and damaged. After that, I wanted my basement straightened out as quickly as possible, so I placed my surviving (and more treasured) possessions on the basement floor—which were then damaged eight years later during the second flooding. With the second clear out, I learned quickly I could live without these more treasured items. I don’t recommend flooding, but it could be imagined to allow more ruthless triage on our mostly unused belongings.

Boschetti, M. A. (1995). Attachment to Personal Possessions: An Interpretive Study of the Older Person’s Experience. Journal of Interior Design, 21(1), 1-12. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-1668.1995.tb00203.x

Coleman, T., & Wiles, J. (2020). Being with objects of meaning: Cherished possessions and opportunities to maintain aging in place. The Gerontologist, 60(1), 41-49.

Dozier, M. E., & Ayers, C. R. (2021). Object attachment as we grow older. Current Opinion in Psychology, 39, 105-108.

Magnusson, M. (2020). Dostadning: The Gentle Art of Swedish Death Cleaning. Canongate Books.

1. This post focuses on partially curated and organized collections of important belongings that do not interfere with our life or our living space. It does not address hoarding, which is an indiscriminate accumulation of possessions that impairs movement and functioning in the cluttered spaces.

2. Swedish Death Cleaning or “döstädning” encourages reflection about our possessions and our relationship to these possessions. It also asserts that shedding these possessions benefits our family’s well-being when we are gone. With KonMari, Marie Kondo takes a different approach to the same end, advising people to keep only what sparks joy.

3. Companies that help families sort through and clear out a deceased parent’s home go by several labels: estate cleanout services, estate liquidation services, bereavement cleanout services, or move managers. They offer a range of services, including hosting estate sales, selling valuable items, coordinating charitable donations, cleaning, and hauling away trash.

#4761. Want to Get Closer With Your Spouse? Take on a Wife Carrying Competition.

One couple‘s experience taking on a race that demands they shoulder each others’ burdens—literally.

DANNY AND KATIE Young are both active, but they’re not exactly the type of couple that stakes out dates on their calendar for the next Hyrox doubles race. Over the last few years, however, both went through separate fitness journeys. So on Christmas Day 2025 when Danny's older brother, Dylan, asked if they had heard of a wild event called wife carrying, they felt ready to take on a new challenge together.

Danny and Katie watched YouTube clips of the North American Wife Carrying Championship, an annual race held every October at the Sunday River Resort in Newry, Maine. It’s exactly what the name implies: a 278-yard race where husbands carry their wives on their backs. This is not the only one of its kind—similar events are staged around the globe and there’s a world championship in Finland—and competition isn’t limited to only married or man-woman couples. The Youngs scrolled through videos of couples running a steep obstacle course, jumping hurdles and sloshing through mud pits all while struggling to stay upright to the finish. The Youngs decided they wanted to take on the event in the coming year.

“One, because it’s so silly and ridiculous,” Katie tells Men’s Health. “Two, we used to live in Boston and we wanted to get back up to New England. The competition (held October 10 this year) was right around our 16th wedding anniversary, so we figured, what better way to celebrate?”

“We are seize the moment people–even if the moment is 10 months in advance,” Danny adds. “Signing up for the competition also felt like a natural celebratory culmination of what we’d done in the last year. We felt like: this is just the sort of thing we’ve been getting ready for. Let’s go do that, to applaud a really cool year of physical and health transformation.”

DANNY AND KATIE met when they were 14 years old, dated in high school, and got married shortly after graduating college. Now 38, they live on a hobby homestead outside of Asheville, NC. Their day jobs (Danny works as a manager at Trader Joe’s, Katie is a clinical supervisor for a community mental health clinic) and taking care of their daughter, Opal, and their small farm leaves little time for traditional training.

But Katie and Danny have navigated the challenges that come with maintaining fitness through both the busy schedules of everyday life and unexpected circumstances. In August of 2023, Katie had ankle surgery and was non-weight bearing for 14 weeks. She gained more than 100 pounds, which was difficult to manage on her 5’3’’ frame. By Thanksgiving of 2023, she started walking with a crutch, but she wasn’t able to return to her workouts (mostly hot yoga) until the summer of 2024. She loves power flows, hot HIIT classes, and hot lifts. “If it’s not over 100 degrees, I’m not interested,” Katie says. “I like that it’s balance, strength, and there’s a cardio element at times.” Twice a week turned to four times a week and then six; by the summer of 2026, she had lost 120 pounds.

Danny had been a CrossFit devotee in his 20s. His job at Trader Joe’s is very physical, picking up and carrying 20 to 50 pound boxes throughout the day. He had abandoned his gym habit in his late 20s; by 30, he struggled with back problems. He returned to the gym three years ago, alternating between calisthenics and foundational compound lifts. He trained twice a week, then three times, then every day. He, too, spent the last year transforming his body from a “dad bod” to one chiseled with muscles—and in top shape, stands at 6’3” and weighs 185 pounds.

But in June of this year, Danny injured his back during a deadlift session. He didn’t lift any weights for the rest of the summer. The couple were still committed to take on the wife carrying contest—but they needed to find a new way to train. They leaned on their active lifestyle on the homestead. They keep four goats, and Katie found that carrying two five-gallon buckets of water up and down the farm’s hills several times a week increased her strength. Katie often picked up one of the 80-pound goats to “escort her out of my garden, where she wants to eat my pumpkins.”

When Danny carried the buckets, he’d sometimes throw Katie on his back. He also carried her around the house and up and down the hills near the farm. They discussed which carry style might work best for them, trying piggyback, upside-down, and other methods. They never attempted a full 278-yard training run, instead opting for spontaneous moments of carrying when circumstances allowed.

“I really like the dual challenge of it, which appeals to both of us,” Danny says. “It’s like a test of a relationship alongside a physical feat. Silly, physical antics are part of our love language.”

RACE MORNING IN Newry, Maine brought clear, blue skies and strong winds. Almost five dozen couples warmed up by jogging up and down the rolling hills of the Sunday River Ski Resort ski slope, navigating sections of the 278-yard course and attempting the log hurdle in the carry position. That’s one of the two dry obstacles on the course; the other is a sand trap.

Danny and Katie watched other couples warming up and did some light stretching. Danny pumped out several sets of pushups as they waited. Hundreds of spectators lined the course.

“The community element seemed really fun,” Katie says afterward. “I can see why a lot of people watch it every year, or why people participate every year.” They met a couple who’d traveled from Utah to compete. Another pair had participated every year for the last 25, while others were in their 60s.

An M.C. announced each set of couples, who competed against one another in rounds of two and for time; the fastest two teams from the qualifying rounds would compete head-to-head in a final heat to determine the winner. A record 58 couples had signed up to compete.

Finally, it was their turn. Katie and Danny wished good luck to their co-competitors, and after several false starts as the MC adjusted his mic, the couples took off. Danny jogged as Katie held on to him utilizing a variation of the popular “Estonian carry,” where she was positioned upside-down, facing his back, using her arms to grip her own legs, which were wrapped over his shoulders like a yolk. The strength and balance she’d built through yoga showed as she held steady, despite Danny’s wobbles on the uneven terrain. She relied on core strength primarily, but also her arms and inner thighs to stay in position.

“It turns out that holding on to your own legs like an upside down human backpack while your partner runs uphill, clambers over a log hurdle, and wades through mud is much harder than it looks,” Katie says. “You’ve got to crunch up as tight as you can, squeeze your legs around your partner, wrap your arms into your own legs, and brace your core; all the while feeling your blood rushing to your head. I think the only reason I was able to do it is from the strength, endurance, and flexibility I’ve gained from my hot yoga practice. Plus, if you can tolerate exercising in a 105 degree room, what’s a little bit of mud?”

The pair didn’t talk much during the race itself. “Most of the race, the noise I was making was something along the lines of, ‘this is so much harder than I thought it was gonna be,’” Danny recalls.

Katie felt the early section had gone well, even though she admittedly couldn’t see anything but the landscape passing below her. “And then, all of a sudden, I can see the ground is moving a lot slower, and Danny's panting and saying how hard it is,” she says.

Still, they kept moving, navigating a steep uphill and then descending toward the mud pit, the course’s final challenge also known as the “Widow-Maker.” Katie had photographed the mud pit prior to the race and texted her friends with the caption, “My fate.”

Danny stepped into the mud hole, navigating the first big step downward. He wobbled. Katie, sensing his unsteadiness, didn’t want to be dropped on her neck and head. “So I abandoned ship,” she says. She threw herself into the cold, wet mud, which filled her mouth and covered her eyes and nose. “It was a pretty solid belly flop,” she added. The muddy water coated her body, officially making the Youngs the first full “mud drop” out of the 30-plus couples that had competed up to that point.

“As I felt her coming off of my back, I thought, ‘where is she going?’” Danny adds afterward.

Katie stood up, wet and laughing so hard she needed a moment to steady herself. The plan had been for Katie to carry Danny across the finish line–but after they cleared the mud pit and stepped onto dry land, he was so wet and she was laughing so hard, she couldn't quite grip him. She jumped onto him, piggy-back, as they emerged from the mud pit and jogged the final yards to the finish line. Just before crossing, she hopped off his back and picked him up, carrying Danny across the finish, laughing as the crowd cheered.

The winning couple was celebrating their 10th anniversary, and their children joined them in crossing the finish line. Most of the competitors stayed through the full two-hour event, as did the spectators, watching the award ceremony and cheering for the various additional contests (best dressed couple and other superlatives.) The winning couple received the wife's weight in beer and five times her weight in cash. Volunteers handed out beers to the entrants. Katie changed out of her wet clothes before they joined his parents, Dylan and his wife, Kristen, and Katie and Danny’s 8-year-old daughter, Opal.

In carrying Danny across the finish, Katie wanted to reinforce what Opal had learned: “Mommy and Daddy are both strong and capable, and there’s no difference,” Katie says.

OVERALL, THE BIGGEST takeaway from the race had little to do with their time or the physical challenge that came with hauling one another across the course. Their relationship, they say, has always been strong—and attempting a fun, unique competition reinforced the tenets of their partnership: fun, laughter, strength, and supporting each other.

Danny suggested they enter again next year, “which I’m definitely up for, competition-wise,” Katie says. “I want to do many ridiculous competitions with you,” Danny adds. “Our relationship quality has been great, and this added another fun adventure.”

After the race, Danny considered how he might approach training for their next attempt. “If we were to run it back, I would definitely add hill sprints to my routine,” he says. “I should have prepared for the fact that the race is very short and very intense. Interval sprints and sled pushing would have been more aligned with the demands of the competition.”

But nothing, in his opinion, is better than replicating the real challenge of the event: carrying a partner and working together. “Spend as much time as possible with your wife on your back,” he says. “It's kooky and fun, and there's nothing else that quite mimics the awkwardness of two spouses becoming one athlete.”
